extracted.intended_audience: political thinkers, legislators, and students of constitutional/governmental design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and historical lessons for forming stable republican governments (mixing orders, checks and balances, separation of powers), illustrated with ancient Greek examples and specific legislative prescriptions attributed to Charondas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of different orders and decisive balances
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures of different orders, and decisive balances, are necessary to preserve mankind from the horrible calamities which revolutions always bring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues the unitability (unreliability) of simple governments and therefore 'the greater necessity of mixtures of different orders, and decisive balances' to prevent revolutions and cyclical degenerations among monarchy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny. Examples and references to Plato and Aristotle are used to support this claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers with three branches and a strong executive
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a strong and independent executive in a single person, and three branches in the legislature instead of two, with equality among the three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an improvement (credited to the English) over ancient practice: 'The necessity of a strong and independent executive in a single person, and of three branches in the legislature instead of two, and of an equality among the three, are improvements made by the English.' This is advanced as the institutional design best able to resist passions and prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power must be opposed to power; interest to interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Power must be opposed to power, and interest to interest, so that orders of men watch over each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the only security for preserving law and liberty: 'orders of men, bound by their interests to watch over each other, and stand the guardians of the laws.' The historical failures of relying on morals, education, or religion alone are cited to justify institutional countervails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions over education or religion alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, religion, oaths, laws, etc., give way before passions and interest; only institutional orders, checks, and balances effectively restrain men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that while education/religion may help in small communities, for great nations they are 'totally inadequate' and that only structured institutional arrangements (orders and balances) can secure lives, liberties, and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative structure with executive, senate, and house and independent negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent civil wars and endless contentions among subordinate cities and a capital, there should be a governor (executive), a senate, and a house of representatives composed of equitable deputies, with each branch possessing an independent negative in the legislature while the whole executive is in the governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific structural recommendation is given as a remedy for Theban/Boetian internal divisions: equitable provincial representation and institutional vetoes are proposed to avoid factions aligning with outside powers and to keep smaller towns from seceding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude remarried fathers from public councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who, having children, shall marry a second time shall be excluded from all public councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to 'mortify their children with the authority of a step-mother' — this is presented as a preventive check on family-derived conflicts influencing public office (listed as Charondas' regulation #1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public humiliation punishment for calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: All who are convicted of calumny shall be conducted through the streets crowned with tamarin (a punishment so infamous that several committed suicide rather than submit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as Charondas' regulation #2; presented as a severe deterrent against slander and political defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit society with wicked men
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit all society with wicked men on the premise that the disposition to evil is strong and many who love virtue are drawn into vice by secret seductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charondas' regulation #3—an early anti-corruption/social-association rule intended to prevent moral contagion and preserve civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sponsored basic literacy for youths
rubrics_metrics.description: All the sons of every family shall learn to write and read under masters in the pay of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charondas' regulation #4; the author praises this law as one 'alone has merit enough to consecrate to immortality the memory of this legislator, and deserves to be imitated by every free people at least.' It is advanced as a core civic-policy requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of orphan property administration and upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of orphans shall be administered by the relations by the father, but their persons and education entrusted to those by the mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charondas' regulation #5; a rule allocating guardianship responsibilities between paternal kin for assets and maternal kin for upbringing, intended to protect orphan interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonor punishment for military cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who refuse to take arms for their country, or quit their ranks in the army, instead of being punished by death, shall be exposed three days in a public square of the city in women's clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charondas' regulation #6; a dishonor-based, public-shaming penalty designed as a less-lethal but severe deterrent against shirking military duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid proposals to change the laws; prioritize the law over criminals' rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit all proposals of changes in the laws; in trials silence criminals who substitute turns of eloquence and arbitrary interpretations for the letter of the laws, asking 'Whether you shall save the law or the criminal?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charondas' regulation #7; this prescriptive rule stresses deference to the written law over persuasive appeals by defendants, and forbids legislative destabilization by constant proposals to alter statutes.
